# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why1: Picking who asks the questions comes right before the link goes out, and the hint already says every question is also written on screen, which is the first thing I'd check for deaf and hard-of-hearing people.
screens.why2: The hint says Keel records a voice, but it's a video interviewer and I picked 'the face', so 'records the voice you pick once for 400 credits' takes a second read to work out what is being recorded and paid for.
screens.why3: I can play two five-second clips and pick one, so this is plainly my own call.
screens.why4: Two voices is a complete choice for most studies, but for my people the missing option is the one I'd want: text-first or captions-led with the voice secondary, or no spoken voice at all.
screens.why5: It keeps my actor wording, 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults', and nothing of AirCaps or the glasses leaks into what respondents will see.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Every question is on screen with live captions, and they can type or tap: Daphne / Saskia / Text only, no voice.

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers answer belongs right after choosing who asks the questions and right before sending, so it is obvious why it comes here.
screens.why2: Each option says in plain words what the respondent will see and do, and 'AI interviewer', 'read and tap' and 'let them choose' need no second read.
screens.why3: I know my wearers well enough to judge whether a spoken video interviewer or a written form suits deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, so I can answer this from my own knowledge.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover the real choices; Daphne writing every question on screen keeps even the spoken option usable for my people, and my pick, Read and tap, is there.
screens.why5: My pick, Read and tap, is shown as I chose it, and nothing of AirCaps or its roles leaks into the wording.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how people answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: The three choices are plain to me as a founder: people I know, a Keel contacts list, or one open link posted in a group.
screens.why3: I know who I can reach, whether that is deaf and hard-of-hearing people I already talk with or a community group I could post in.
screens.why4: The three ways of reaching people are distinct and cover my real choices, and my pick (people I know by name) is there; no escape chip is needed for a routing choice.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes my study; it only asks how the links go out.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits under the title, and each card puts its deciding count, 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, right beside its own 'Holding up'.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on this page, but each card line says what was counted (said yes, would have gone better, would do it), over how many (7) and where the bar sits (5 of 7), so I take it in at once.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry the belief lines I checked word for word, though the solution statement above them is garbled ('the wearer ... the app ... shows ... and gets back' the same captions twice) and reads like a broken sentence, not my mechanism.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what three holding beliefs mean for AirCaps or what to do next (move to the commercial stage, look into the 3 who would wear the glasses only on a condition); the only explanatory line just describes how the verdict is computed.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, but the page never says 7 is a small sample for a clean 7 of 7 on all three beliefs, and it counts the 3 'on a condition' adopters as 'would do it' without saying what the condition was.
screens.instead: Your solution is holding up on all three beliefs, though with only 7 people answering; 3 of the 7 would wear the glasses only on a condition, so open Adoption friction to see what it is before you go on to price.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside the number that decides it, 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart shows Yes 4 and Yes, with some steps 3 for me and No 0 against, over 7 people, and the strip puts the marker at 5 with 'no more than 1 in 3 say no' spelled out, so all three things are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Compatibility and the belief line, 'For most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults, their phone was with them and online', is word for word what I checked, and the question uses the fact's three answers, not 'only with help'.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me concretely that the phone being with them and online won't stop my customers and that adoption friction is where to look next, which matches the borrow-a-pair and demo comments underneath.
screens.why_b5: The count line keeps n=7 visible and says 'a lean, not a call', but the So line states flatly that the phone 'is not what will stop them' from seven people, and the 'One more thing · Compatibility' quotes are really about trying a demo pair, not about the phone.
screens.instead: With all 7 having their phone with them and online, a lean from a small group, the phone is unlikely to be what stops them, so look at adoption friction below, where three asked to try a pair first.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 saying it would have gone better, all 7 a lot, against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts who said better (7, split 7 a lot and 0 a little), the strip shows 7 cells, and the marker sits at 5 of 7 with the 1-in-3 rule beside it, all plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The card says Relative advantage and carries my benefit, following more without asking anyone to repeat, word for word as I checked it, awkward grammar included.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates that all 7 imagined it going better and points to Adoption friction; it never says what a unanimous 'a lot better' means for me, such as leading with this benefit or confirming it in a real trial.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible at 7, the screen flags it as a small group (a lean, not a call) and as a hypothetical asked with AirCaps in mind, and it never calls the result strong.
screens.instead: All 7 who answered said AirCaps would have made their last conversation a lot better. That is a lean from a small group, imagined rather than tried, so lead with this benefit and check it on real 15-day trial wearers; whether they would wear the glasses is Adoption friction, below.

screens.why_b1: The card says Holding up next to 7 of 7 would do it against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, all seven cells are for me, and the marker at 5 shows the bar, which is plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The card's name is Adoption friction and its belief is 'Most would wear the glasses, paired to the phone', word for word what I checked.
screens.why_b4: The So line points 'below' for what would make it worth it to the 3. Below I find only the same 'don't look odd in conversation' condition again and Tomás's end-seat quote, which is about something else, so it never says plainly that how the glasses look across a table is what I have to get right.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the count line says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and the 3 conditional yeses are split from the 4 plain ones rather than folded into a bare 7 of 7.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 would wear them as they are, and the other 3 only if the glasses don't look odd in conversation. A lean, not a call, but the look across the table is the catch to test next, with more people.

screens.why_b1: Each box states its verdict ("Compatibility held, 7 of 7", "Adoption friction held, 7 of 7") with the 7 of 7 and the bar of 5 of 7 beside it, so I know both lines held and on what count.
screens.why_b3: Both belief lines are word for word the ones I checked: phone with them and online, and wearing the glasses paired to the phone.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do next; the quotes point to a demo or borrow-a-pair step before ordering, a check on readability under stage lights, and pickup of audience questions in a big hall, but the screen never draws any of that out.
screens.why_b5: Seven people is never called a small sample, and the counts don't add up: Harriet and Ruth are listed as 'never saw' the adoption question yet quoted under Compatibility, and only 1 of the '3 on a condition' is shown.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add things I didn't type: people want a trial pair before ordering, lens readability under stage lights, capturing audience questions beyond the front speaker, and a one-sided-deaf user whose end-seat workaround already 'works most of the time'.
screens.instead: Say plainly that 7 of 7 is seven people, and turn what they added into next steps: offer a demo or borrow-a-pair before ordering, test the lens under stage lights and in big halls with audience questions, and note that one-sided hearing loss may already have a workaround.

screens.why1: As the first screen it makes sense to check whether I actually have conversations with hearing people regularly before asking me anything about them.
screens.why2: It's plain to me; I would say yes straight away, since most of my days involve hearing people at work, in shops and in my family.
screens.why3: I know exactly how often I talk with hearing people, so I can answer it from my own week.
screens.why4: For a weekly-habit gate, yes and no cover it cleanly, and the screener needs no escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks to me, but the founder's segment says deaf or hard-of-hearing adults in the US, and only the weekly talking part is checked here.
screens.why6: It is short and easy to hear once, though 'I'll read 2 options' is more than a yes-or-no needs; 'Yes or no' would say it better.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with hearing people here in the US? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether I actually lost the thread of one of those conversations this week.
screens.why2: "Lose track of a conversation" is exactly how I'd say it; it happens at dinners, at work, at the counter, and I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know whether I lost the thread in a conversation with hearing people in the last seven days; that's my own week.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and the chips only belong to the story box after a Yes, so they don't muddy the gate.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, an app or the company's plans reaches me; it just asks about losing track, which is the problem and not just being in a conversation.
screens.why6: One short sentence followed by "Yes or no" is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The gate asks about the costly event (losing track) within the window as one act; a deaf person who followed fine with lipreading or a good setup can truly say No, so both answers are possible, no escape is offered, and the founder's band can be supported or refuted.

screens.why1: The study has just asked whether I lost track of a conversation with hearing people this week, so showing me an idea about following those conversations is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses and eye contact are all words I use every day; the only stumble is the odd phrase 'an app on lightweight glasses', but I still get it on first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what it is to look down at captions on my phone and lose the speaker's face and lips, so I can judge this from my own life.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options shown.
screens.why5: The product is named and described on purpose as the idea, in plain words, and nothing of the founder's own terms for people like me reaches me.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it says the same thing twice, with 'lightweight glasses' and 'inside the lens' each repeated, so the second sentence is a mouthful that adds nothing to the first.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, lightweight glasses that show live captions of what people nearby are saying, inside the lens. The people building it believe it would mean you could read the words while still looking at the person talking.

screens.why1: After the glasses card I expected a question about following the conversation with captions, so asking only whether my phone was there feels a little off to the side.
screens.why2: Phone with you and online is plain to me, though 'your last conversation' is loose and could mean any chat, not one with hearing people.
screens.why3: I know whether my phone was on me and had signal; it nearly always is.
screens.why4: 'Yes, with some steps' is odd for whether my phone was on me and online; it either was or it was not, unless it means turning data on.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but the founder's idea rests on reading live captions on glasses in a fast or noisy talk, and this asks only about the phone, so the meaning has drifted.
screens.why6: It is short, asks one thing, gives three options I can hold, and ends with one escape.
screens.why7: Nearly every deaf or hard-of-hearing adult in the US has their phone with them and online, so everyone answers Yes; the belief cannot be refuted, and the step the pitch depends on, wearing glasses and following captions as people talk, is not tested.
screens.instead: On your last conversation with hearing people that was hard to follow, could you have kept reading captions while watching their faces? Yes, easily / Yes, most of the time / Only sometimes / No / I can't tell

screens.why1: I said my phone was online only with some steps, so asking what those steps were is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: It reads my own answer back the way I gave it, and 'having your phone online' is how I'd think about turning on data or finding wifi before a chat.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I did to get my phone working for that conversation, whether that was switching on data, finding wifi or charging it.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, with no options to judge.
screens.why5: It stays on my phone and my conversation, and nothing of the company's product or its words for people slips in beyond the idea card I already saw.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it's two short sentences with one question and nothing to hold in my head.
screens.instead: You said yes, with some steps. What did you have to do to get your phone online for that conversation?

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the phone question, it makes sense to ask whether captions in glasses would have helped me.
screens.why2: I understand it on first hearing, though I would say keep up with a conversation rather than follow and join one.
screens.why3: I know exactly how my last conversations with hearing people went, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover every answer I could give, and I can't tell fits as the escape.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's own description of AirCaps reaches me, and the job is in plain words, with nothing of the founder's plan leaking.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options and one escape, easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: The measure, the four fixed options, the balance and the escape are all right, but the occasion is any recent conversation rather than one that was too fast or noisy to follow, so the hard case the advantage is for is bent.
screens.instead: Think of the last time a conversation with hearing people was too fast or too noisy to follow. Would AirCaps have helped you keep up better, or not? A lot better, A little better, No difference, Worse, or I can't tell.

screens.why1: After being shown the glasses and asked whether they'd beat my last conversation, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually put them on and use them.
screens.why2: Wearing glasses paired to my phone is plain to me; I pair hearing aids and other gadgets to my phone all the time.
screens.why3: Whether I'd wear captioning glasses in front of hearing people is something only I can answer, from my own conversations.
screens.why4: The four answers run cleanly from yes to no, and the condition about looking odd is a real worry for me, not a filler yes. I can't tell fits as the escape.
screens.why5: It is the idea card's own glasses and captions, with no company plan or jargon reaching me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options and one escape, easy to hold after hearing it once.
screens.why7: Wearing the paired glasses is a habit I take on myself, the four answers split two for and two against, the condition is specific to this step, and I can't tell sits apart as the card requires.

screens.why1: It comes after the glasses question but does not point back to what I said there, so I can't tell if it's following up my answer on wearing them or on whether it would help, which makes it feel a bit abrupt.
screens.why2: The words are plain, but with no link back to my answer and with 'worth it' when I've never been told a price, I'd have to work out what it is asking me to weigh.
screens.why3: I can say what would make captions on glasses useful in a noisy room with hearing people, but whether it's 'worth it' depends on a cost I haven't seen, so part of my answer would be a guess.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: It only names AirCaps, which the idea card already showed me, and nothing of the founder's own terms comes through.
screens.why6: One short question that is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: You said whether you'd wear the glasses paired to your phone. What would they need to do in a fast or noisy conversation for you to wear them every week?
